title: Confusion, precision, recall and F1

what.formal: Given a classifier and a labelled test set, the **confusion matrix** is a table whose rows are the true classes and whose columns are the predicted classes; the entry in row $i$, column $j$ counts the examples whose true class is $i$ and whose predicted class is $j$. For one chosen class $k$, write $TP$ (true positives) for its examples predicted as $k$, $FP$ (false positives) for examples of other classes predicted as $k$, and $FN$ (false negatives) for examples of class $k$ predicted as something else. Then the **precision** of class $k$ is $TP/(TP+FP)$, its **recall** is $TP/(TP+FN)$, and its **F1** is the harmonic mean of the two, $2\,PR/(P+R)$.
what.plain: Precision asks: of the examples the model labelled class k, how many really were class k? Recall asks: of the examples that really were class k, how many did the model find? F1 is a single number that is large only when both are large.

what.md: **Why one accuracy number is not enough.** Accuracy collapses the matrix to a single count: it says how many predictions were right, not where the wrong ones went. A model can reach a given accuracy by making its errors on one class, on another, or spread evenly, and those are different failures. The confusion matrix keeps the detail; precision, recall and F1 are three ways of summarising one class's row and column of it.

head: Quantity
Formula
The question it answers
rows: Of all examples, how many did the model get right?
When the model says class k, how often is it right?
When the truth is class k, how often does the model catch it?
Is the model good at both of the above at once?

what.note: Precision divides by the number of times the model *claimed* class $k$ — everything the model put in that column. It drops whenever the model over-predicts a class.

gloss.md: examples that truly are class $k$ and were predicted as class $k$ — the hits
examples of some other class predicted as class $k$ — the false alarms
the share of the model's class-$k$ predictions that turned out correct

what.note: Recall divides by the number of examples that *truly* are class $k$ — the whole row. It drops whenever the model misses instances of a class.

gloss.md: the same hits as in precision
examples that truly are class $k$ but were predicted as something else — the misses
the share of the true class-$k$ examples the model found

what.note: F1 is the **harmonic mean** of precision and recall, not their ordinary average. The harmonic mean is small whenever either term is small: precision $1.0$ with recall $0.0$ gives F1 $= 0$, whereas the ordinary average would give $0.5$. That is the whole reason F1 is used — it refuses to reward a model that is good at only one of the two.

gloss.md: one number that is large only when both precision and recall are large

what.md: **Macro-averaging versus micro-averaging.** A confusion matrix with $K$ classes gives $K$ precisions, $K$ recalls and $K$ F1 values. To report one number you average, and there are two standard ways. **Macro-averaging** takes the plain, unweighted mean of the per-class values: every class counts equally, so a class with $10$ examples weighs as much as one with $1000$. **Micro-averaging** pools the counts first — add up all $TP$, all $FP$ and all $FN$ across the classes, then compute one precision and one recall from those totals. In single-label classification, where each example belongs to exactly one class, the pooled $TP$ is the number of correct predictions and both pooled denominators are the number of examples, so micro-precision, micro-recall and micro-F1 all equal the accuracy. Macro and micro therefore agree only when the classes are balanced; on skewed data macro-F1 sits below accuracy.

**Two misconceptions.** First, F1 is not a better accuracy. It ignores true negatives altogether — examples the model correctly leaves out of a class contribute to nothing — and its harmonic mean weights precision and recall equally, which is a choice rather than a law. F1 is the right instrument for a single class, often a rare one; it is the wrong instrument for an overall score on balanced data. Second, "the F1 of a multi-class model" is not a defined quantity: without saying macro or micro, the number could be either, and the two disagree by as much as the class imbalance.

**When these break.** Precision is undefined for a class the model never predicts, because its denominator is zero; recall is undefined for a class that does not appear in the test set. Implementations return zero or a warning, and either way the value is a convention rather than a measurement. F1 is meaningful only for a single class or as an average with a stated rule, and it says nothing about the classes a model correctly ignores, so it cannot stand in for accuracy when false positives on the negative class matter.

example.md: **Example 1 — two classes, one matrix.** A test set has $40$ cats and $60$ dogs. Of the $40$ cats the model calls $35$ cats and $5$ dogs; of the $60$ dogs it calls $15$ cats and $45$ dogs. Rows are truth, columns are prediction:

items.md: Accuracy is the sum of the diagonal divided by the total: $35 + 45 = 80$, so accuracy $= 80/100 = 0.80$.
items.why: The diagonal holds the correct predictions. Off-diagonal entries are errors, and accuracy ignores which off-diagonal they sit on.

items.md: For Cat, $TP = 35$, $FP = 15$ (dogs called cats) and $FN = 5$ (cats called dogs). Precision $= 35/(35+15) = 35/50 = 0.70$; recall $= 35/(35+5) = 35/40 = 0.875$.
items.why: Precision divides by the column total — everything predicted Cat. Recall divides by the row total — everything truly Cat. Swapping row and column is the most common error with this matrix.
Macro-F1 is the plain mean of the two per-class values. With classes of a similar size it stays close to accuracy ($0.80$ here) — the second example shows what happens when they are not.

example.md: **Example 2 — three classes of unequal size.** Same layout, three classes A, B and C, with rows true and columns predicted:

items.md: Accuracy is the diagonal over the total: $50 + 15 + 5 = 70$, so accuracy $= 70/100 = 0.70$.
items.why: The three classes have $60$, $30$ and $10$ examples — unequal, which is what makes the next steps differ from each other.

items.md: Per-class precision and recall. A: precision $50/62 = 0.806$, recall $50/60 = 0.833$. B: precision $15/26 = 0.577$, recall $15/30 = 0.500$. C: precision $5/12 = 0.417$, recall $5/10 = 0.500$.
items.why: Every precision divides by that class's column total ($62$, $26$, $12$); every recall divides by its row total ($60$, $30$, $10$). The rare class C has the lowest precision because a handful of its column's entries come from other classes.
The harmonic mean punishes the weaker of the two numbers, which is why class C's F1 ($0.4545$) sits well below its recall ($0.500$).

items.md: Macro-F1 is their unweighted mean: $(0.8197 + 0.5357 + 0.4545)/3 = 1.8099/3 = 0.603$. Micro-F1 pools the counts first: pooled $TP = 70$, pooled $FP$ and pooled $FN$ each total $30$ over $100$ examples, so micro-precision $=$ micro-recall $= 70/100 = 0.700$, and micro-F1 $= 0.700$ — the accuracy again.
items.why: The two averaging rules disagree here: macro-F1 is $0.603$, micro-F1 is $0.700$, a gap of about 9.7 points. Macro counts the small class C as heavily as the large class A, so it falls; micro lets the large class dominate, so it reproduces accuracy.

example.md: One model, one test set, and four numbers: accuracy $0.700$, macro-F1 $0.603$, micro-F1 $0.700$, and a rare-class F1 of $0.4545$. Which of these is *the* score is exactly the question card 3 settles.

quiz.q: For a single class, what does recall measure?

opts.md: The share of the examples that truly belong to that class which the model managed to find
opts.expl: Correct. Recall divides the class's true positives by the whole true row — every example that really is that class. It drops when the model misses instances of the class.

opts.md: The share of the model's predictions of that class which turned out to be correct
opts.expl: That is precision. It divides by the column — everything the model claimed to be that class. Choosing precision where recall was meant is the row-versus-column confusion again.

opts.md: The share of all test examples the model labelled correctly
opts.expl: That is accuracy, which counts every class together rather than looking at one class's row.

quiz.q: A three-class confusion matrix has rows (true) and columns (predicted): true X gives [40, 5, 5], true Y gives [4, 20, 6], true Z gives [1, 4, 15]. What is the recall of class Z?
quiz.hint: Recall of a class divides the examples it predicted correctly by the total number of examples that truly belong to it — the row, not the column.
quiz.sol: Class Z's row totals to 1 + 4 + 15 = 20, of which 15 are predicted correctly. Recall = 15/20 = 0.75. For contrast, precision for Z would divide by the column total, 5 + 6 + 15 = 26, giving 15/26 ≈ 0.577 — a different number from the same row and column.

quiz.q: A model never predicts class D, although class D is present in the test set. What are class D's precision and recall?

opts.expl: Recall is indeed 0 — none of the true class-D examples were found. But precision is not 0; it is a fraction with a zero denominator, because the model made no class-D predictions at all.

opts.md: Precision is undefined and recall is 0
opts.expl: Correct. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) becomes 0/0 when the model never predicts the class, so it is undefined rather than zero. Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 0/(true count), which is genuinely 0. Libraries return a convention (often 0) and warn, which is why a zero here should be read as "no measurement".
Recall has a non-zero denominator — the number of true class-D examples — so it is well defined and equals 0. Only precision has the 0/0 problem.

quiz.q: The same model, on the same test set, reports micro-F1 $0.70$ and macro-F1 $0.60$. What does the gap tell you?

opts.md: The model performs unevenly across classes: it does better on the larger classes, which dominate micro-F1, than on the smaller ones, which macro-F1 weighs equally heavily
opts.expl: Correct. Micro-F1 pools the examples, so frequent classes drive it; macro-F1 weights each class equally, so rare classes pull it down. A gap this size means the rare classes are where the errors sit.

opts.md: The two numbers describe different models, so they cannot be compared
opts.expl: Both numbers were computed on the same model and the same test set. They differ because of the averaging rule, not because of a change in the model.

opts.md: Macro-F1 is always lower than micro-F1, so the gap is expected and carries no information
opts.expl: The two coincide when the classes are balanced, and on some datasets macro-F1 comes out higher. The direction of the gap is not automatic; here it reflects a real difference in per-class performance.

close: **Where this is going:** precision, recall and the two F1s give a per-class and a per-example view of the same confusion matrix. Card 3 turns these into a decision rule for which number to report — and closes the section with its skip check.
